'''Abdominal aortic aneurysm''' ('''AAA''') is a localized enlargement of the [[abdominal aorta]] such that the diameter is greater than {{convert|3|cm|abbr=on}} or more than 50% larger than normal.<ref name=Kent2014>{{cite journal |author=Kent KC |title=Clinical practice. Abdominal aortic aneurysms. |journal=[[The New England Journal of Medicine]] |volume=371 |issue=22 |pages=2101–2108 |date=27 November 2014 |pmid=25427112 |doi=10.1056/NEJMcp1401430}}</ref> An AAA usually causes no symptoms, except during rupture.<ref name=Kent2014/> Occasionally, abdominal, back, or leg pain may occur.<ref name=AFP2006>{{cite journal |vauthors=Upchurch GR, Schaub TA |title=Abdominal aortic aneurysm |journal=[[American Family Physician]] |volume=73 |issue=7 |pages=1198–1204 |year=2006 |pmid=16623206}}</ref> Large aneurysms can sometimes be felt by pushing on the abdomen.<ref name=AFP2006/> [[Aortic rupture|Rupture]] may result in [[pain in the abdomen]] or [[Back pain|back]], [[hypotension|low blood pressure]], or [[Syncope (medicine)|loss of consciousness]], and often results in death.<ref name=Kent2014/><ref name=Spa2014>{{cite journal |vauthors=Spangler R, Van Pham T, Khoujah D, Martinez JP |title=Abdominal emergencies in the geriatric patient. |journal=International Journal of Emergency Medicine |volume=7 |issue=1 |article-number=43 |year=2014 |pmid=25635203 |pmc=4306086 |doi=10.1186/s12245-014-0043-2 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

<!-- Causes and diagnosis -->
AAAs occur most commonly in men, those over 50, and those with a family history of the disease.<ref name=Kent2014/> Additional risk factors include [[smoking]], [[hypertension|high blood pressure]], and other [[cardiovascular disease|heart or blood vessel diseases]].<ref name=Wit2011>{{cite journal |author=Wittels K |title=Aortic emergencies. |journal=[[Emergency Medicine Clinics of North America]] |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=789–800, vii |date=November 2011 |pmid=22040707 |doi=10.1016/j.emc.2011.09.015}}</ref> Genetic conditions with an increased risk include [[Marfan syndrome]] and [[Ehlers–Danlos syndromes|Ehlers–Danlos syndrome]].<ref name=CDC2014/> AAAs are the most common form of [[aortic aneurysm]].<ref name=CDC2014/> About 85% occur below the [[kidney]]s, with the rest either at the level of or above the kidneys.<ref name=Kent2014/> In the [[United States]], [[screening (medicine)|screening]] with [[abdominal ultrasound]] is recommended for males between 65 and 75 years of age with a history of smoking.<ref name=USP2014>{{cite journal |author=LeFevre ML |title=Screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation statement. |journal=[[Annals of Internal Medicine]] |volume=161 |issue=4 |pages=281–290 |date=19 August 2014 |pmid=24957320 |s2cid=265875637 |doi=10.7326/m14-1204 |doi-access=}}</ref> In the [[United Kingdom]] and [[Sweden]], screening all men over 65 is recommended.<ref name=Kent2014/><ref name=Sv2014>{{cite journal |last1=Svensjö |first1=S |last2=Björck |first2=M |last3=Wanhainen |first3=A |title=Update on screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm: a topical review. |journal=[[European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery]] |volume=48 |issue=6 |pages=659–667 |date=December 2014 |pmid=25443524 |doi=10.1016/j.ejvs.2014.08.029 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Once an aneurysm is found, further ultrasounds are typically done regularly because aneurysms grow,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sage Journals: Discover world-class research |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/action/cookieAbsent |access-date=2026-05-02 |website=Sage Journals |language=en |doi=10.1177/15385744241265758?utm_source=researchgate.net&utm_medium=article}}</ref> and monitoring to identify when an aneurysm meets a threshold for repair <ref name=AFP2006/>

<!-- Prevention and treatment -->
Abstinence from cigarette smoking is the single best way to prevent the disease.<ref name=Kent2014/> Other methods of prevention include treating high blood pressure, treating [[hypercholesterolemia|high blood cholesterol]], and avoiding being [[overweight]].<ref name=Kent2014/> Surgery is usually recommended when the diameter of an AAA grows to >5.5 cm in males and >5.0 cm in females.<ref name=Kent2014/> Other reasons for repair include symptoms and a rapid increase in size, defined as more than one centimeter per year.<ref name=AFP2006/> Repair may be either by [[Open aortic surgery|open surgery]] or [[endovascular aneurysm repair]] (EVAR).<ref name=Kent2014/> As compared to open surgery, EVAR has a lower risk of death in the short term and a shorter hospital stay, but may not always be an option.<ref name=Kent2014/><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Thomas DM, Hulten EA, Ellis ST, Anderson DM, Anderson N, McRae F, Malik JA, Villines TC, Slim AM | title = Open versus Endovascular Repair of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm in the Elective and Emergent Setting in a Pooled Population of 37,781 Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. | journal = ISRN Cardiology | volume = 2014 | article-number = 149243 |year = 2014 | pmid = 25006502 | doi=10.1155/2014/149243 | pmc=4004021| doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Biancari F, Catania A, D'Andrea V | title = Elective endovascular vs. open repair for abdominal aortic aneurysm in patients aged 80 years and older: systematic review and meta-analysis. | journal = European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery | volume = 42 | issue = 5 | pages = 571–6 | date = November 2011 | pmid = 21820922 | doi=10.1016/j.ejvs.2011.07.011| doi-access = free }}</ref> There does not appear to be a difference in longer-term outcomes between the two.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Paravastu SC, Jayarajasingam R, Cottam R, Palfreyman SJ, Michaels JA, Thomas SM | title = Endovascular repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm. | journal = [[The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews]] | volume = 1 | issue = 1 | article-number = CD004178 | date = 23 January 2014 | pmid = 24453068 | doi=10.1002/14651858.CD004178.pub2| pmc = 10749584 }}</ref> Repeat procedures are more common with EVAR.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Ilyas S, Shaida N, Thakor AS, Winterbottom A, Cousins C | title = Endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) follow-up imaging: the assessment and treatment of common postoperative complications. | journal = Clinical Radiology | volume = 70 | issue = 2 | pages = 183–196 | <!-- Prognosis and epidemiology -->
AAAs affect 2–8% of males over the age of 65.<ref name=Kent2014/> They are five times more common in men.<ref name=Kumar2020>{{cite book |last1=Bunce|first1=Nicholas H. |last2=Ray |first2=Robin|last3=Patel|first3=Hitesh |editor1-last=Feather |editor1-first=Adam |editor2-last=Randall |editor2-first=David |editor3-last=Waterhouse |editor3-first=Mona |title=Kumar and Clark's Clinical Medicine |date=2020 |publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-7020-7870-5 |pages=1129–1130 |edition=10th |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sl3sDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA1129 |chapter=30. Cardiology}}</ref> In those with an aneurysm less than 5.5 cm, the risk of rupture in the next year is below 1%.<ref name=Kent2014/> Among those with an aneurysm between 5.5 and 7 cm, the risk is about 10%, while for those with an aneurysm greater than 7 cm the risk is about 33%.<ref name=Kent2014/> [[Mortality rate|Mortality]] if ruptured is 85% to 90%.<ref name=Kent2014/> Globally, aortic aneurysms resulted in 168,200 deaths in 2013, up from 100,000 in 1990.<ref name=GBD2015De>{{cite journal|author=((GBD 2015 Mortality and Causes of Death Collaborators)) |title=Global, regional, and national life expectancy, all-cause mortality, and cause-specific mortality for 249 causes of death, 1980–2015: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2015.|journal=Lancet|date=8 October 2016|volume=388|issue=10053|pages=1459–1544|pmid=27733281|doi=10.1016/s0140-6736(16)31012-1|pmc=5388903}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | title = Global, regional, and national age-sex specific all-cause and cause-specific mortality for 240 causes of death, 1990-2013: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2013 | journal = Lancet | date = 17 December 2014 | pmid = 25530442 | doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(14)61682-2 | volume=385 | issue=9963 | pages=117–71 | pmc=4340604| author = ((GBD 2013 Mortality Causes of Death Collaborators)) }}</ref> In the United States AAAs resulted in between 10,000 and 18,000 deaths in 2009.<ref name=CDC2014>{{cite web |title=Aortic Aneurysm Fact Sheet|url=https://www.cdc.gov/dhdsp/data_statistics/fact_sheets/fs_aortic_aneurysm.htm|website=cdc.gov|access-date=3 February 2015 |date=July 22, 2014|url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150203095250/http://www.cdc.gov/dhdsp/data_statistics/fact_sheets/fs_aortic_aneurysm.htm |archive-date=3 February 2015}}</ref>

==Signs and symptoms==
[[File:Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Location.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Abdominal aortic aneurysm location]]
The vast majority of aneurysms are asymptomatic. However, as the abdominal aorta expands and/or ruptures, the aneurysm may become painful and lead to pulsating sensations in the [[abdomen]] or [[Chest pain|pain in the chest]], [[Low back pain|lower back]], [[Pain|legs]], or [[Scrotal pain|scrotum]].<ref name="harrisons">{{cite book|last=Fauci|first=Anthony|title=Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine|publisher=McGraw-Hill Professional|date=2008-03-06|edition=17|chapter=242|isbn=978-0-07-146633-2}}</ref>

===Complications===
The complications include rupture, peripheral [[embolization]], acute aortic occlusion, and aortocaval (between the aorta and [[inferior vena cava]]) or aortoduodenal (between the aorta and the [[duodenum]]) [[fistulae]]. On physical examination, a [[palpable]] and pulsatile abdominal mass can be noted. [[Bruit]]s can be present in case of renal or visceral arterial [[stenosis]].<ref name=emedicine/>

The signs and symptoms of a ruptured AAA may include severe pain in the lower back, flank, abdomen, or [[Groin pain|groin]]. A mass that pulses with the heartbeat may also be felt.<ref name=Spa2014/> The bleeding can lead to a [[hypovolemic shock]] with [[hypotension|low blood pressure]] and a [[tachycardia|fast heart rate]], which may cause [[Syncope (medicine)|fainting]].<ref name=Spa2014/> The mortality of AAA rupture is as high as 90 percent. 65 to 75 percent of patients die before they arrive at the hospital and up to 90 percent die before they reach the operating room.<ref name=SmallAneurysmTrial>{{cite journal |vauthors=Brown LC, Powell JT | title = Risk Factors for Aneurysm Rupture in Patients Kept Under Ultrasound Surveillance | journal = Annals of Surgery | volume = 230 | issue = 3 | pages = 289–96; discussion 296–7 | date = September 1999 | pmid = 10493476 | pmc = 1420874 | doi = 10.1097/00000658-199909000-00002 }}</ref> The bleeding can be [[wikt:retroperitoneal|retroperitoneal]] or into the [[intraperitoneal|abdominal cavity]]. Rupture can also create a connection between the aorta and intestine or [[inferior vena cava]].<ref name=Treska>Treska V. ''et al.'':Aneuryzma břišní aorty, Prague, 1999, {{ISBN|80-7169-724-9}}</ref> Flank [[ecchymosis]] (appearance of a bruise) is a sign of retroperitoneal [[hemorrhage|bleeding]] and is also called [[Grey Turner's sign]].<ref name=emedicine/><ref name=Cecil>{{cite book |last=Goldman |first=Lee |title=Goldman's Cecil Medicine |publisher=Elsevier Saunders |location=Philadelphia, PA |date=25 July 2011 |edition=24th |page=837 |isbn=978-1-4377-2788-3}}</ref>

==Causes==
The exact causes of the degenerative process remain unclear. There are, however, some hypotheses and well-defined [[risk factors]].<ref name="pmid25884861">{{cite journal |vauthors=Keisler B, Carter C |title=Abdominal aortic aneurysm |journal=Am Fam Physician |volume=91 |issue=8 |pages=538–543 |date=April 2015 |pmid=25884861}}</ref>
* Tobacco smoking: More than 90% of people who develop an AAA have [[Health effects of tobacco|smoked]] at some point in their lives.<ref name="Greenhalgh RM, Powell JT 2008 494–501">{{cite journal |vauthors=Greenhalgh RM, Powell JT |title=Endovascular repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm |journal=N. Engl. J. Med. |volume=358 |issue=5 |pages=494–501 |date=January 2008 |pmid=18234753 |doi=10.1056/NEJMct0707524}}</ref>
* Alcohol and hypertension: The inflammation caused by prolonged use of alcohol and hypertensive effects from abdominal edema which leads to [[hemorrhoids]], [[esophageal varices]], and other conditions, is also considered a long-term cause of AAA.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022}}
* Genetic influences: The influence of genetic factors is high. AAA is four to six times more common in male siblings of known patients, with a risk of 20–30%.<ref name=siblings>{{cite journal |vauthors=Baird PA, Sadovnick AD, Yee IM, Cole CW, Cole L |title=Sibling risks of abdominal aortic aneurysm |journal=Lancet |volume=346 |issue=8975 |pages=601–604 |date=September 1995 |pmid=7651004 |s2cid=27523622 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(95)91436-6}}</ref> The high familial prevalence rate is most notable in male individuals.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Clifton MA |title=Familial abdominal aortic aneurysms |journal=Br J Surg |volume=64 |issue=11 |pages=765–766 |date=November 1977 |pmid=588966 |s2cid=40560333 |doi=10.1002/bjs.1800641102}}</ref> There are many hypotheses about the exact genetic disorder that could cause a higher incidence of AAA among male members of the affected families. Some have presumed that the influence of [[alpha 1-antitrypsin]] deficiency could be crucial, while other experimental works favor the hypothesis of [[X-linked]] [[mutation]], which would explain the lower incidence in [[heterozygous]] females. Other hypotheses of genetic causes have also been formulated.<ref name=emedicine/> [[Connective tissue]] disorders, such as Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and [[Loeys–Dietz syndrome|Loeys-Dietz syndrome]], have also been strongly associated with AAA.<ref>{{Citation |last=Loeys |first=Bart L. |title=Loeys-Dietz Syndrome |date=1993 |work=GeneReviews® |editor-last=Adam |editor-first=Margaret P. |url=http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1133/ |access-date=2026-03-04 |place=Seattle (WA) |publisher=University of Washington, Seattle |pmid=20301312 |last2=Dietz |first2=Harry C. |editor2-last=Bick |editor2-first=Sarah |editor3-last=Mirzaa |editor3-first=Ghayda M. |editor4-last=Pagon |editor4-first=Roberta A.}}</ref><ref name=Treska/> Both [[relapsing polychondritis]] and [[pseudoxanthoma elasticum]] may cause abdominal aortic aneurysm.<ref name="Bolognia">{{cite book |last1=Rapini |first1=Ronald P. |last2=Bolognia |first2=Jean L. |last3=Jorizzo |first3=Joseph L. |title=Dermatology: 2-Volume Set |publisher=Mosby |location=St. Louis, Missouri |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-4160-2999-1}}</ref>
* Atherosclerosis: The AAA was long considered to be caused by [[atherosclerosis]] because the walls of the AAA frequently carry an atherosclerotic burden. However, this hypothesis cannot explain the initial defect and the development of [[Vascular occlusion|occlusion]], which is observed in the process.<ref name=emedicine/> Another hypothesis is that plaque buildup can cause a feed-forward dysfunction in the signaling among neurons that regulate pressure in the aorta. This feed-forward process leads to an over-pressuring condition that ruptures the aorta.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Conley |first1=Buford R. |last2=Doux |first2=John D. |last3=Lee |first3=Patrick Y. |last4=Bazar |first4=Kimberly A. |last5=Daniel |first5=Stephanie M. |last6=Yun |first6=Anthony J. |title=Integrating the theories of Darwin and Bernoulli: Maladaptive baroreceptor network dysfunction may explain the pathogenesis of aortic aneurysms |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306987705001507 |journal=Medical Hypotheses |volume=65 |issue=2 |pages=266–272 |date=1 January 2005 |issn=0306-9877 |pmid=15922098 |doi=10.1016/j.mehy.2005.03.006|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* Other causes of the development of AAA include: [[infection]], [[Physical trauma|trauma]], [[arteritis]], and [[cystic medial necrosis]].<!-- (m. Erdheim). --><ref name=Treska/>

==Pathophysiology==
[[File:Aortadiagramgray.png|thumb|A plate from ''[[Gray's Anatomy]]'' with yellow lines depicting the most common infrarenal location of the AAA]]
[[File:Aortic Aneurism 76F 3D SR Nevit Dilmen.stl|thumb|3D file showing an aortic aneurysm]]
The most striking [[histopathology|histopathological]] changes of the aneurysmatic aorta are seen in the [[tunica media]] and [[intima]] layers. These changes include the accumulation of lipids in [[foam cells]], extracellular free [[cholesterol]] crystals, [[calcification]]s, [[thrombosis]], and [[venous ulcer|ulcerations]] and ruptures of the layers. [[Adventitial]] [[inflammation|inflammatory]] [[Infiltration (medical)|infiltrate]] is present.<ref name=Treska/> However, the [[Chemical decomposition|degradation]] of the tunica media by means of a [[proteolytic]] process seems to be the basic [[pathophysiology|pathophysiologic]] mechanism of AAA development. Some researchers report increased expression and activity of matrix [[metalloproteinase]]s in individuals with AAA. This leads to the elimination of [[elastin]] from the media, rendering the aortic wall more susceptible to the influence of [[blood pressure]].<ref name=emedicine/> Other reports have suggested the [[serine protease]] [[granzyme B]] may contribute to aortic aneurysm rupture through the cleavage of [[decorin]], leading to disrupted [[collagen]] organization and reduced tensile strength of the adventitia.<ref name="pmid20035050">{{cite journal |vauthors=Chamberlain CM, Ang LS, Boivin WA, Cooper DM, Williams SJ, Zhao H, Hendel A, Folkesson M, Swedenborg J, Allard MF, McManus BM, Granville DJ | title = Perforin-independent extracellular granzyme B activity contributes to abdominal aortic aneurysm | journal = Am. J. Pathol. | volume = 176 | issue = 2 | pages = 1038–49 | year = 2010 | pmid = 20035050 | pmc = 2808106 | doi = 10.2353/ajpath.2010.090700 }}</ref><ref name="pmid21900960">{{cite journal |vauthors=Ang LS, Boivin WA, Williams SJ, Zhao H, Abraham T, Carmine-Simmen K, McManus BM, Bleackley RC, Granville DJ | title = Serpina3n attenuates granzyme B-mediated decorin cleavage and rupture in a murine model of aortic aneurysm | journal = Cell Death Dis | volume = 2 | issue = 9| pages = e209 | year = 2011 | pmid = 21900960 | pmc = 3186906 | doi = 10.1038/cddis.2011.88 }}</ref> There is also a reduced amount of [[vasa vasorum]] in the abdominal aorta (compared to the thoracic aorta); consequently, the tunica media must rely mostly on diffusion for nutrition, which makes it more susceptible to damage.<ref name="MacSweeney">{{cite journal |vauthors=MacSweeney ST, Powell JT, Greenhalgh RM | title = Pathogenesis of abdominal aortic aneurysm | journal = Br J Surg | volume = 81 | issue = 7 | pages = 935–41 | year = 1994 | pmid = 7922083 | s2cid = 21272785 | doi = 10.1002/bjs.1800810704}}</ref>

[[Hemodynamics]] affect the development of AAA, which has a [[wikt:predilection|predilection]] for the [[wikt:infrarenal|infrarenal]] aorta. The histological structure and mechanical characteristics of the infrarenal aorta differ from those of the [[thoracic aorta]]. The diameter decreases from the root to the [[aortic bifurcation]], and the wall of the infrarenal aorta also contains a lesser proportion of [[elastin]]. The mechanical [[Muscle tension|tension]] in the abdominal aortic wall is therefore higher than in the thoracic aortic wall. The [[Elasticity (physics)|elasticity]] and [[wikt:distensibility|distensibility]] also decline with age, which can result in gradual [[wikt:dilatation|dilatation]] of the segment. Higher [[intraluminal]] pressure in patients with arterial hypertension markedly contributes to the progression of the pathological process.<ref name=Treska/> Suitable hemodynamic conditions may be linked to specific intraluminal thrombus (ILT) patterns along the aortic lumen, which in turn may affect AAA's development.<ref name="Biasetti">{{cite journal |vauthors=Biasetti J, Hussain F, Gasser TC | title = Blood flow and coherent vortices in the normal and aneurysmatic aortas: a fluid dynamical approach to intra-luminal thrombus formation | journal = J R Soc Interface | volume = 8 | issue = 63 | pages = 1449–61 | year = 2011 | pmid = 21471188 | pmc = 3163425 | doi = 10.1098/rsif.2011.0041 }}</ref>

==Diagnosis==
An abdominal aortic aneurysm is usually diagnosed by [[physical exam]], [[abdominal ultrasound]], or [[CT scan]]. Plain abdominal radiographs may show the outline of an aneurysm when its walls are calcified. However, the outline will be visible by X-ray in less than half of all aneurysms. Ultrasonography is used to screen for aneurysms and to determine their size if present. Additionally, free peritoneal fluid can be detected. It is non-invasive and sensitive, but the presence of bowel gas or obesity may limit its usefulness.<ref name="pmid39055063">{{cite journal |vauthors=Lu F, Lin Y, Zhou J, Chen Z, Liu Y, Zhong M, Wang L |title=Obesity and the obesity paradox in abdominal aortic aneurysm |journal=Front Endocrinol (Lausanne) |volume=15 |issue= |article-number=1410369 |date=2024 |pmid=39055063 |pmc=11269098 |doi=10.3389/fendo.2024.1410369 |doi-access=free |url=}}</ref> CT scan has nearly 100% sensitivity for an aneurysm and is also useful in preoperative planning, detailing the anatomy and possibility for endovascular repair. In the case of suspected rupture, it can also reliably detect retroperitoneal fluid. Alternative less often used methods for visualization of an aneurysm include [[MRI]] and [[angiography]].<ref name="pmid29979239">{{cite journal |vauthors=Green DB, Palumbo MC, Lau C |title=Imaging of Thoracoabdominal Aortic Aneurysms |journal=J Thorac Imaging |volume=33 |issue=6 |pages=358–365 |date=November 2018 |pmid=29979239 |doi=10.1097/RTI.0000000000000341 |url=}}</ref>

An aneurysm ruptures if the mechanical stress (tension per area) exceeds the local wall strength; consequently, peak wall stress (PWS),<ref name="Fillinger_2003">{{cite journal |vauthors=Fillinger MF, Marra SP, Raghavan ML, Kennedy FE |title=Prediction of rupture risk in abdominal aortic aneurysm during observation: wall stress versus diameter |journal=Journal of Vascular Surgery |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=724–732 |date=April 2003 |pmid=12663969 |doi=10.1067/mva.2003.213 |doi-access=free}}</ref> mean wall stress (MWS),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chung |first1=Timothy K. |last2=Gueldner |first2=Pete H. |last3=Kickliter |first3=Trevor M. |last4=Liang |first4=Nathan L. |last5=Vorp |first5=David A. |date=November 2022 |title=An Objective and Repeatable Sac Isolation Technique for Comparing Biomechanical Metrics in Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms |journal=Bioengineering |volume=9 |issue=11 |page=601 |doi=10.3390/bioengineering9110601 |pmid=36354512 |pmc=9687639 |issn=2306-5354|doi-access=free}}</ref> and peak wall rupture risk (PWRR)<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Gasser TC, Auer M, Labruto F, Swedenborg J, Roy J |title=Biomechanical rupture risk assessment of abdominal aortic aneurysms: model complexity versus predictability of finite element simulations |journal=Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg |volume=40 |issue=2 |pages=176–185 |year=2010 |pmid=20447844 |doi=10.1016/j.ejvs.2010.04.003 |doi-access=free}}</ref> are more reliable parameters than diameter to assess AAA rupture risk. Medical software allows computing these rupture risk indices from standard clinical CT data and provides a patient-specific AAA rupture risk diagnosis.<ref>{{cite web |title=VASCOPS |url=http://www.vascops.com/en/vascops-A4clinics.html |url-status=live |access-date=15 January 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717185318/http://www.vascops.com/en/vascops-A4clinics.html |archive-date=17 July 2011}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last1=Canchi |first1=Tejas |last2=Patnaik |first2=Sourav S. |last3=Nguyen |first3=Hong N. |last4=Ng |first4=E.Y.K. |last5=Narayanan |first5=Sriram |last6=Muluk |first6=Satish C. |last7=De Oliveira |first7=Victor |last8=Finol |first8=Ender A. |title=A Comparative Study of Biomechanical and Geometrical Attributes of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms in the Asian and Caucasian Populations |journal=Journal of Biomechanical Engineering |volume=142 |issue=6 |date=1 June 2020 |article-number=061003 |issn=1528-8951 |pmid=31633169 |s2cid=204813645 |pmc=10782868 |doi=10.1115/1.4045268}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{cite journal |last1=Rengarajan |first1=Balaji |last2=Patnaik |first2=Sourav S. |last3=Finol |first3=Ender A. |title=A Predictive Analysis of Wall Stress in Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms Using a Neural Network Model |journal=Journal of Biomechanical Engineering |volume=143 |issue=12 |date=1 December 2021 |article-number=121004 |issn=1528-8951 |pmid=34318314 |pmc=8420793 |doi=10.1115/1.4051905}}</ref> This type of biomechanical approach has been shown to accurately predict the location of AAA rupture.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Doyle BJ, McGloughlin TM, Miller K, Powell JT, Norman PE |title=Regions of high wall stress can predict the future location of rupture in abdominal aortic aneurysm |journal=Cardiovasc Intervent Radiol |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=815–818 |year=2014 |pmid=24554200 |s2cid=35797072 |doi=10.1007/s00270-014-0864-7}}</ref>

Abdominal aortic aneurysms are commonly divided according to their size and symptomatology. An aneurysm is usually defined as an outer aortic diameter over 3 cm (normal diameter of the [[aorta]] is around 2 cm),<ref name=ACCAHA2022/> or more than 50% of normal diameter.<ref name="SolomonKent2014">{{cite journal |last=Kent |first=K. Craig |title=Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |date=27 November 2014 |volume=371 |issue=22 |pages=2101–2108 |doi=10.1056/NEJMcp1401430 |pmid=25427112}}</ref> If the outer diameter exceeds 5.5 cm, the aneurysm is considered to be large.<ref name=screening/> Ruptured AAA should be suspected in any person older than 60 who experiences collapse, unexplained low blood pressure, or sudden-onset back or abdominal pain. Abdominal pain, shock, and a pulsatile mass are only present in a minority of cases.{{citation needed|date=June 2022}} Although an unstable person with a known aneurysm may undergo surgery without further imaging, the diagnosis will usually be confirmed using CT or ultrasound scanning.{{citation needed|date=October 2021}}

The suprarenal aorta normally measures about 0.5 cm larger than the infrarenal aorta.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uptodate.com/contents/clinical-features-and-diagnosis-of-abdominal-aortic-aneurysm|title=Clinical features and diagnosis of abdominal aortic aneurysm|author=Jeffrey Jim, Robert W Thompson|website=[[UpToDate]]|date=2018-03-05|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180330212246/https://www.uptodate.com/contents/clinical-features-and-diagnosis-of-abdominal-aortic-aneurysm|archive-date=2018-03-30}}</ref>

===Differential diagnosis===
Aortic aneurysm rupture may be mistaken for the [[renal colic|pain of kidney stones]], or [[muscle related back pain]].<ref name=Spa2014/>

==Management==
The treatment options for asymptomatic AAA are [[wikt:conservative treatment|conservative]] management, surveillance with a view to eventual repair, and immediate repair. Two modes of repair are available for an AAA: [[Open aortic surgery|open aneurysm repair]], and endovascular aneurysm repair ([[EVAR]]). An intervention is often recommended if the aneurysm grows more than 1 cm per year or it is bigger than 5.5 cm.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Ulug |first1=Pinar |last2=Powell |first2=Janet T |last3=Martinez |first3=Melissa Ashley-Marie |last4=Ballard |first4=David J |last5=Filardo |first5=Giovanni |title=Surgery for small asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysms |journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |date=1 July 2020 |volume=2020 |issue=7 |article-number=CD001835 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD001835.pub5 |pmid=32609382 |pmc=7389114 }}</ref> Repair is also indicated for symptomatic aneurysms. Ten years after open AAA repair, the overall survival rate was 59%.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Timmers |first1=Tim K. |last2=van Herwaarden |first2=Joost A. |last3=de Borst |first3=Gert-Jan |last4=Moll |first4=Frans L. |last5=Leenen |first5=Luke P. H. |title=Long-Term Survival and Quality of Life After Open Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Repair |journal=World Journal of Surgery |date=December 2013 |volume=37 |issue=12 |pages=2957–2964 |doi=10.1007/s00268-013-2206-3 |pmid=24132818 |s2cid=9019195}}</ref> Mycotic abdominal aorta aneurysm (MAAA) is a rare and life-threatening condition. Because of its rarity, there is a lack of adequately powered studies and consensus on its treatment and follow-up. A management protocol on the management of mycotic abdominal aortic aneurysm was recently published in the Annals of Vascular Surgery by Premnath et al.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Premnath |first1=Sivaram |last2=Zaver |first2=Vasudev |last3=Hostalery |first3=Aurelien |last4=Rowlands |first4=Timothy |last5=Quarmby |first5=John |last6=Singh |first6=Sanjay |date=2021-07-01 |title=Mycotic Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms – A Tertiary Centre Experience and Formulation of a Management Protocol |url=https://www.annalsofvascularsurgery.com/article/S0890-5096(21)00079-0/abstract |journal=Annals of Vascular Surgery |volume=74 |pages=246–257 |doi=10.1016/j.avsg.2020.12.025 |issn=0890-5096 |pmid=33508457|s2cid=231760989|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Conservative===
Conservative management is indicated in people where repair carries a high mortality risk and in patients where repair is unlikely to improve life expectancy. The mainstay of the conservative treatment is [[tobacco smoking|smoking]] cessation.{{citation needed|date=October 2021}}

Surveillance is indicated in small asymptomatic aneurysms (less than 5.5 cm) where the risk of repair exceeds the risk of rupture.<ref name=":0" /> As an AAA grows in diameter, the risk of rupture increases. Surveillance until an aneurysm has reached a diameter of 5.5 cm has not been shown to have a higher risk as compared to early intervention.<ref name=SmallAneurysm>{{cite journal |vauthors=Powell JT, Brown LC, Forbes JF, Fowkes FG, Greenhalgh RM, Ruckley CV, Thompson SG | title = Final 12-year follow-up of surgery versus surveillance in the UK Small Aneurysm Trial | journal = Br J Surg | volume = 94 | issue = 6 | pages = 702–8 | date = Jun 2007 | pmid = 17514693 | doi = 10.1002/bjs.5778 | s2cid = 25392801 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=ADAM>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lederle FA, Wilson SE, Johnson GR, Reinke DB, Littooy FN, Acher CW, Ballard DJ, Messina LM, Gordon IL, Chute EP, Krupski WC, Busuttil SJ, Barone GW, Sparks S, Graham LM, Rapp JH, Makaroun MS, Moneta GL, Cambria RA, Makhoul RG, Eton D, Ansel HJ, Freischlag JA, Bandyk D | title = Immediate repair compared with surveillance of small abdominal aortic aneurysms | journal = N Engl J Med | volume = 346 | issue = 19 | pages = 1437–44 | date = May 2002 | pmid = 12000813 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMoa012573 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Medication===
No medical therapy has been proven to be effective at decreasing the growth rate or rupture rate of asymptomatic AAAs,<ref name="Kent2014" /> though observational data suggest [[statin]]s may attenuate both growth rate and risk of surgery.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Skovbo Kristensen |first=Joachim S. |last2=Krasniqi |first2=Lytfi |last3=Obel |first3=Lasse M. |last4=Kavaliunaite |first4=Egle |last5=Liisberg |first5=Mads |last6=Lindholt |first6=Jes S. |date=2024-04-01 |title=Exploring Drug Re-Purposing for Treatment of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S107858842300967X |journal=European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery |language=en |volume=67 |issue=4 |pages=570–582 |doi=10.1016/j.ejvs.2023.11.037}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=American Heart Association Journals |url=https://www.ahajournals.org/action/cookieAbsent |access-date=2026-04-07 |website=American Heart Association Journals |language=en |doi=10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.125.074544}}</ref> [[Blood pressure]] and [[lipids]] should, however, be treated per usual. The use of [[statin]]s in moderate or high intensity in patients with [[Atherosclerosis|atherosclerotic]] AAAs reduces the risk of adverse events such as [[myocardial infarction]] and [[stroke]].<ref name="ACCAHA2022"/>

====Open repair====
{{Main|Open aortic surgery}}

Open repair is indicated in young patients as an elective procedure, or in growing or large, symptomatic or ruptured aneurysms. The aorta must be clamped during the repair, denying blood to the abdominal organs and sections of the [[spinal cord]]; this can cause a range of complications. As it is essential to perform the critical part of the operation quickly, the incision is typically made large enough to facilitate the fastest repair. Recovery after open AAA surgery takes significant time. The minimums are a few days in intensive care, a week total in the hospital, and a few months before full recovery.{{citation needed|date=September 2021}}

====Endovascular repair====
[[File:Endovasc.jpg|thumb|Abdominal aortic endoprosthesis, CT scan, original aneurysm marked in blue]]
{{Main|Endovascular aneurysm repair}}

Endovascular repair first became practical in the 1990s and although it is now an established alternative to open repair, its role is yet to be clearly defined. It is generally indicated in older, high-risk patients or patients unfit for open repair. However, endovascular repair is feasible for only a portion of AAAs, depending on the morphology of the aneurysm. The main advantages over open repair are that there is less peri-operative mortality, less time in [[intensive care]], less time in hospital overall, and an earlier return to normal activity. Disadvantages of endovascular repair include a requirement for more frequent ongoing hospital reviews and a higher chance of further required procedures. According to the latest studies, the EVAR procedure does not offer any benefit for overall survival or health-related [[quality of life]] compared to open surgery, although aneurysm-related mortality Although the current standard of determining rupture risk is based on maximum diameter, it is known that smaller AAAs that fall below this threshold (diameter<5.5 cm) may also rupture, and larger AAAs (diameter>5.5 cm) may remain stable.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Darling RC, Messina CR, Brewster DC, Ottinger LW | title = Autopsy study of unoperated abdominal aortic aneurysms. The case for early resection | journal = Circulation | volume = 56 | issue = 3 Suppl | pages = II161–4 | date = September 1977 | pmid = 884821 }}</ref><ref name=pmid9808857>{{cite journal |vauthors=Nicholls SC, Gardner JB, Meissner MH, Johansen HK | title = Rupture in small abdominal aortic aneurysms | journal = Journal of Vascular Surgery | volume = 28 | issue = 5 | pages = 884–8 | date = November 1998 | pmid = 9808857 | doi = 10.1016/S0741-5214(98)70065-5 | doi-access = free }}</ref> In one report, it was shown that 10–24% of ruptured AAAs were less than 5 cm in diameter.<ref name=pmid9808857/> It has also been reported that of 473 non-repaired AAAs examined from autopsy reports, there were 118 cases of rupture, 13% of which were less than 5 cm in diameter. This study also showed that 60% of the AAAs greater than 5 cm (including 54% of those AAAs between 7.1 and 10 cm) never experienced rupture.<ref name="Vorp DA 2007 1887–902">{{cite journal | author = Vorp DA | title = Biomechanics of abdominal aortic aneurysm | journal = Journal of Biomechanics | volume = 40 | issue = 9 | pages = 1887–902 | year = 2007 | pmid = 17254589 | pmc = 2692528 | doi = 10.1016/j.jbiomech.2006.09.003 }}</ref> Vorp ''et al.'' later deduced from the findings of Darling ''et al.'' that if the maximum diameter criterion were followed for the 473 subjects, only 7% (34/473) of cases would have died from rupture before surgical intervention as the diameter was less than 5 cm, with 25% (116/473) of cases possibly undergoing unnecessary surgery since these AAAs may never have ruptured.<ref name="Vorp DA 2007 1887–902"/>

Alternative methods of rupture assessment have been recently reported. The majority of these approaches involve the numerical analysis of AAAs using the common engineering technique of the finite element method (FEM) to determine the wall stress distributions. Recent reports have shown that these stress distributions have been shown to correlate to the overall geometry of the AAA rather than solely to the maximum diameter.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Vorp DA, Raghavan ML, Webster MW | title = Mechanical wall stress in abdominal aortic aneurysm: influence of diameter and asymmetry | journal = Journal of Vascular Surgery | volume = 27 | issue = 4 | pages = 632–9 | date = April 1998 | pmid = 9576075 | doi = 10.1016/S0741-5214(98)70227-7 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Sacks MS, Vorp DA, Raghavan ML, Federle MP, Webster MW | title = In vivo three-dimensional surface geometry of abdominal aortic aneurysms | journal = Annals of Biomedical Engineering | volume = 27 | issue = 4 | pages = 469–79 | year = 1999 | pmid = 10468231 | doi = 10.1114/1.202 | s2cid = 21394944 }}</ref><ref name="Doyle BJ, Callanan A, Burke PE, et al. 2009 443–54">{{cite journal |vauthors=Doyle BJ, Callanan A, Burke PE, Grace PA, Walsh MT, Vorp DA, McGloughlin TM | title = Vessel Asymmetry as an Additional Diagnostic Tool in the Assessment of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms | journal = Journal of Vascular Surgery | volume = 49 | issue = 2 | pages = 443–54 | date = February 2009 | pmid = 19028061 | pmc = 2666821 | doi = 10.1016/j.jvs.2008.08.064 }}</ref> It is also known that wall stress alone does not completely govern failure as an AAA will usually rupture when the wall stress exceeds the wall strength. ==Epidemiology==
The occurrence of AAA varies by ethnicity. In the United Kingdom, the rate of AAA in Caucasian men older than 65 years is about 4.7%, while in Asian men it is 0.45%.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Salem MK, Rayt HS, Hussey G, Rafelt S, Nelson CP, Sayers RD, Naylor AR, Nasim A | title = Should Asian men be included in abdominal aortic aneurysm screening programmes? | journal = Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg | volume = 38 | issue = 6 | pages = 748–9 | date = December 2009 | pmid = 19666232 | doi = 10.1016/j.ejvs.2009.07.012 | doi-access = free | hdl = 2381/7912 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> It is also less common in individuals of African, and Hispanic heritage.<ref name=Kent2014/> They occur four times more often in men than in women.<ref name=Kent2014/>

There are at least 13,000 deaths yearly in the U.S. secondary to AAA rupture.<ref name=Kent2014/> The peak [[incidence (epidemiology)|number of new cases per year]] among males is around 70 years of age, and the [[prevalence|percentage of males affected]] over 60 years is 2–6%. The frequency is much higher in smokers than in non-smokers (8:1), and the risk decreases slowly after [[smoking cessation]].<ref name=smoking>{{cite journal |vauthors=Wilmink TB, Quick CR, Day NE | title = The association between cigarette smoking and abdominal aortic aneurysms | journal = J Vasc Surg | volume = 30 | issue = 6 | pages = 1099–105 | date = Dec 1999 | pmid = 10587395 | doi = 10.1016/S0741-5214(99)70049-2 | doi-access = free }}</ref> In the U.S., the incidence of AAA is 2–4% in the adult population.<ref name=emedicine>{{eMedicine|med|3443|Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm}}</ref>

Rupture of the AAA occurs in 1–3% of men aged 65 or more, for whom the mortality rate is 70–95%.<ref name=screening>{{cite journal |vauthors=Lindholt JS, Juul S, Fasting H, Henneberg EW | title = Screening for abdominal aortic aneurysms: single centre randomised controlled trial | journal = BMJ | volume = 330 | issue = 7494 | page = 750 | date = Apr 2005 | pmid = 15757960 | pmc = 555873 | doi = 10.1136/bmj.38369.620162.82 }}</ref>

==History==
The first historical records about AAA are from [[Ancient Rome]] in the 2nd century AD, when Greek surgeon [[Antyllus]] tried to treat the AAA with [[Anatomical terms of location#Proximal and distal|proximal]] and [[Anatomical terms of location#Proximal and distal|distal]] [[Ligature (medicine)|ligature]], central [[Surgical incision|incision]] and removal of [[thrombosis|thrombotic]] material from the [[aneurysm]]. However, attempts to treat the AAA surgically were unsuccessful until 1923. In that year, [[Rudolph Matas]] (who also proposed the concept of endoaneurysmorrhaphy), performed the first successful aortic ligation on a human.<ref name=livesay>{{cite journal |vauthors=Livesay JJ, Messner GN, Vaughn WK | title = Milestones in Treatment of Aortic Aneurysm: Denton A. Cooley, MD, and the Texas Heart Institute | journal = Tex Heart Inst J | volume = 32 | issue = 2 | pages = 130–4 | year = 2005 | pmid = 16107099 | pmc = 1163455 }}</ref> Other methods that were successful in treating the AAA included wrapping the aorta with polyethene [[cellophane]], which induced [[fibrosis]] and restricted the growth of the aneurysm. Endovascular aneurysm repair was first performed in the late 1980s and has been widely adopted in the subsequent decades. Endovascular repair was first used for treating a ruptured aneurysm in Nottingham in 1994.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Yusuf SW, Whitaker SC, Chuter TA, Wenham PW, Hopkinson BR | title = Emergency endovascular repair of leaking aortic aneurysm | journal = Lancet | volume = 344 | issue = 8937 | page = 1645 | date = December 1994 | pmid = 7984027 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(94)90443-X | s2cid = 45648419 }}</ref>

==Research==

===Risk assessment===
There have been many calls for alternative approaches to rupture risk assessment over the past number of years, with many believing that a biomechanics-based approach may be more suitable than the current diameter approach. Numerical modeling is a valuable tool to researchers allowing approximate wall stresses to be calculated, thus revealing the rupture potential of a particular aneurysm. Experimental models are required to validate these numerical results and provide further insight into the biomechanical behavior of the AAA. ''In vivo'', AAAs exhibit a varying range of material strengths<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Raghavan ML, Kratzberg J, Castro de Tolosa EM, Hanaoka MM, Walker P, da Silva ES | title = Regional distribution of wall thickness and failure properties of human abdominal aortic aneurysm | journal = J. Biomech | volume = 39 | issue = 16 | pages = 3010–3016 | year = 2006 | pmid = 16337949 | doi = 10.1016/j.jbiomech.2005.10.021 }}</ref> from localised weak hypoxic regions<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Vorp DA, Lee PC, Wang DH, Makaroun MS, Nemoto EM, Ogawa S, Webster MW | title = Association of intraluminal thrombus in abdominal aortic aneurysm with local hypoxia and wall weakening | journal = Journal of Vascular Surgery | volume = 34 | issue = 2 | pages = 291–299 | year = 2001 | pmid = 11496282 | doi = 10.1067/mva.2001.114813 | doi-access = free }}</ref> to much stronger regions and areas of calcifications.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Speelman L, Bohra A, Bosboom EM, Schurink GW, van de Vosse FN, Makaorun MS, Vorp DA | title = Effects of wall calcifications in patient-specific wall stress analyses of abdominal aortic aneurysms | journal = Journal of Biomechanical Engineering | volume = 129 | issue = 1 | pages = 105–109 | year = 2007 | pmid = 17227104 | doi = 10.1115/1.2401189 }}</ref>

Finding ways to predict future AAA growth is seen as a research priority.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Regent |last2=Jones |first2=Amy |last3=Cassimjee |first3=Ismail |last4=Handa |first4=Ashok |last5=Oxford Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm |first5=Study. |title=International opinion on priorities in research for small abdominal aortic aneurysms and the potential path for research to impact clinical management |journal=International Journal of Cardiology |date=October 2017 |volume=245 |pages=253–255 |doi=10.1016/j.ijcard.2017.06.058 |pmid=28874296 |url=https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:c8773f49-d2a4-44f2-9957-510d39b9d476 }}</ref>

Another related line of research is utilizing mathematical decision modeling (e.g., [[Markov decision processes]]) to determine improved treatment policies. Initial results suggest that a more dynamic policy could provide benefits, although such claims have not been clinically verified.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mattila |first1=Robert |last2=Siika |first2=Antti |last3=Roy |first3=Joy |last4=Wahlberg |first4=Bo |title=2016 IEEE Conference on Control Applications (CCA) |chapter=A Markov decision process model to guide treatment of abdominal aortic aneurysms |date=2016 |pages=436–441 |doi=10.1109/CCA.2016.7587869 |arxiv=1611.02177 |isbn=978-1-5090-0755-4 |s2cid=5632830 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grant |first1=Stuart |last2=Sperrin |first2=Matthew |last3=Carlson |first3=Eric |last4=Chinai |first4=Natasha |last5=Ntais |first5=Dionysios |last6=Hamilton |first6=Matthew |last7=Dunn |first7=Graham |last8=Bunchan |first8=Iain |last9=Davies |first9=Linda |last10=McCollum |first10=Charles |title=Calculating when elective abdominal aortic aneurysm repair improves survival for individual patients: development of the Aneurysm Repair Decision Aid and economic evaluation |journal=Health Technology Assessment |date=2015 |volume=19 |issue=32 |pages=1–154 |doi=10.3310/hta19320 |pmid=25924187 |pmc=4781543 |url=https://www.journalslibrary.nihr.ac.uk/hta/hta19320/#/abstract}}</ref> A study recently showed that aneurysms can be accurately predicted as to whether they are stable (lacking repair or intervention), requiring repair, or at risk of rupture from scans years prior to any event based on a machine-learning based classification tool.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chung |first1=Timothy K. |last2=Gueldner |first2=Pete H. |last3=Aloziem |first3=Okechukwu U. |last4=Liang |first4=Nathan L. |last5=Vorp |first5=David A. |date=9 February 2024 |title=An artificial intelligence based abdominal aortic aneurysm prognosis classifier to predict patient outcomes |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=14 |issue=1 |page=3390 |doi=10.1038/s41598-024-53459-5 |pmid=38336915 |issn=2045-2322|pmc=10858046 |bibcode=2024NatSR..14.3390C}}</ref>

===Prevention and treatment===
An animal study showed that removing a single protein prevents early damage in blood vessels from triggering a later-stage, frequently lethal complication. By eliminating the gene for a signaling protein called cyclophilin A (CypA) from a strain of mice, researchers were able to provide complete protection against abdominal aortic aneurysm.<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Study establishes major new treatment target in diseased arteries |date=May 10, 2009 |magazine=U.S. News & World Report |url=http://www.physorg.com/news161183060.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110606091215/http://www.physorg.com/news161183060.html |archive-date=June 6, 2011 }}</ref>

Other recent research identified Granzyme B ([[GZMB]]) (a protein-degrading enzyme) to be a potential target in the treatment of abdominal aortic aneurysms. Elimination of this enzyme in mice models both slowed the progression of aneurysms and improved survival.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Chamberlain CM, Ang LS, Boivin WA, Cooper DM, Williams SJ, Zhao H, Hendel A, Folkesson M, Swedenborg J, Allard MF, McManus BM, Granville DJ | title = Perforin-Independent Extracellular Granzyme B Activity Contributes to Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm | journal = The American Journal of Pathology | volume = 176 | issue = 2 | pages = 1038–1049 | year = 2010 | pmid = 20035050 | pmc = 2808106 | doi = 10.2353/ajpath.2010.090700 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Discovery points way for new treatment for aneurysms |date=January 27, 2010 |publisher=University of British Columbia |url=http://www.hli.ubc.ca/news_events/news.php?user=events&index=1&count=1&date=20100101 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100219124709/http://www.hli.ubc.ca/news_events/news.php?user=events&index=1&count=1&date=20100101 |archive-date=February 19, 2010 }}</ref>

===Preclinical research===
The mechanisms that lead to AAA development are still not completely understood at a cellular and molecular level. To better understand the pathophysiology of AAA, it is often necessary to use experimental animal models. It is often questioned how well these models translate to human disease. Even though no animal model exactly represents the human condition, all the existing ones focus on one different pathophysiological aspect of the disease. Combining the results from different animal models with clinical research can provide a better overview of the AAA pathophysiology. The most common animal models are rodents (mice and rats), although, for certain studies, such as testing preclinical devices or surgical procedures, large animal models (pig, sheep) are more frequently used. The rodent models of AAA can be classified according to different aspects. There are dissecting models vs non-dissecting models and genetically determined models vs chemically induced models. extract:
Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a localized enlargement of the abdominal aorta such that the diameter is greater than 3 cm (1.2 in) or more than 50% larger than normal. An AAA usually causes no symptoms, except during rupture. Occasionally, abdominal, back, or leg pain may occur. Large aneurysms can sometimes be felt by pushing on the abdomen. Rupture may result in pain in the abdomen or back, low blood pressure, or loss of consciousness, and often results in death.
AAAs occur most commonly in men, those over 50, and those with a family history of the disease. Additional risk factors include smoking, high blood pressure, and other heart or blood vessel diseases. Genetic conditions with an increased risk include Marfan syndrome and Ehlers–Danlos syndrome. AAAs are the most common form of aortic aneurysm. About 85% occur below the kidneys, with the rest either at the level of or above the kidneys. In the United States, screening with abdominal ultrasound is recommended for males between 65 and 75 years of age with a history of smoking. In the United Kingdom and Sweden, screening all men over 65 is recommended. Once an aneurysm is found, further ultrasounds are typically done regularly because aneurysms grow, and monitoring to identify when an aneurysm meets a threshold for repair 
Abstinence from cigarette smoking is the single best way to prevent the disease. Other methods of prevention include treating high blood pressure, treating high blood cholesterol, and avoiding being overweight. Surgery is usually recommended when the diameter of an AAA grows to >5.5 cm in males and >5.0 cm in females. Other reasons for repair include symptoms and a rapid increase in size, defined as more than one centimeter per year. Repair may be either by open surgery or endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR). As compared to open surgery, EVAR has a lower risk of death in the short term and a shorter hospital stay, but may not always be an option. There does not appear to be a difference in longer-term outcomes between the two. Repeat procedures are more common with EVAR.
AAAs affect 2–8% of males over the age of 65. They are five times more common in men. In those with an aneurysm less than 5.5 cm, the risk of rupture in the next year is below 1%. Among those with an aneurysm between 5.5 and 7 cm, the risk is about 10%, while for those with an aneurysm greater than 7 cm the risk is about 33%. Mortality if ruptured is 85% to 90%. Globally, aortic aneurysms resulted in 168,200 deaths in 2013, up from 100,000 in 1990. In the United States AAAs resulted in between 10,000 and 18,000 deaths in 2009.
